Battle of Hampton Roads. On March eighth and ninth, eighteen sixty-two, two revolutionary ironclad warships clashed for the first time in naval history. The Confederate CSS Virginia, formerly the USS Merrimack, and the Union USS Monitor engaged off the coast of Virginia in a battle that would fundamentally transform naval warfare worldwide.

The Virginia was a large armored wooden hull mounting ten guns. On March eighth, it devastated wooden Union warships, destroying the USS Cumberland and burning the USS Congress. Union officers and sailors watched helplessly as cannons bounced off the Virginia's sloped iron armor. It seemed nothing could stop this revolutionary vessel.

The Union blockade of Confederate ports had driven the Confederacy to innovate. They raised and armored the Merrimack as the CSS Virginia. Learning of this, the Union contracted the Monitor—a revolutionary shallow-draft ironclad with a rotating gun turret—in a race against time. Both ships were revolutionary. No wooden navy could withstand them.

On March ninth, the Monitor arrived in darkness and engaged the Virginia at close range. Neither ship could decisively damage the other. The two ships fought for four hours before both withdrew, claiming victory but achieving no clear tactical advantage.

The battle proved that ironclads were the future of naval warfare. Wooden warships were relegated to secondary roles. Within a decade, ironclad battleships were standard for all major navies. The Virginia was scuttled by Confederate forces in May eighteen sixty-two to prevent Union capture. The Monitor sank in a storm later that year.

Hampton Roads marked the death of the wooden warship that had dominated naval warfare for centuries. The battle captured popular imagination as artists and photographers documented the unprecedented sight of ships that seemed invulnerable. For the Union blockade, the inconclusive result was actually favorable. The Virginia, despite its capabilities, could not break the blockade decisively. The Union's industrial capacity ensured it would build more Monitors. The battle demonstrated that the side with greater industrial capacity to innovate and produce would prevail—a theme that played out across the entire war.
